correctness.rationale: The first integrals on the two sides give y³=3β(r²−x²)/(2α) above and (−y)³=3(r²−x²)/(2γ) below. The normal velocities at each nonzero crossing have the same nonzero sign, so the upper and lower graphs concatenate to the stated periodic orbit. Integrating the heights and using |dx|/|ẋ| for elapsed physical time gives the exponents 5/3 and −1/3 in r, respectively; the time singularities of order 2/3 at the endpoints are integrable. Beta recurrence gives B(1/2,4/3)/B(1/2,1/3)=2/5 and the prefactor ratio is 3/2, yielding P/Q=3/5. The lower area/time ratio determines r², the quotient of the upper and lower ratios determines β, and the two areas then separately determine γ and α. This algebra is reversible for every positive observation quadruple, proving both compositions, global realizability and analyticity. Taking logs gives an affine inverse with row absolute sums (6,4,3,1) in order α,β,γ,r. With measurement logs ordered as in the source, the α row is (−2,3/2,−1,−3/2); perturbing along its sign vector realizes the bound exactly. The sharp constant 6 is for inverse Lipschitz stability in maximum logarithmic norm, not the product of the forward and inverse operator norms. Fixing any three of the four channels leaves a family of realizable quadruples and distinct reconstructed inputs, proving the stated restricted minimality. The inspected random checker supports but is not needed for the analytic proof.

value.rationale: The problem uses four directly specified geometric and temporal observables from a single orbit with unknown crossing amplitude. Separate residence times and half-areas allow inference that total period alone does not: they separate the upper normal velocity factor from amplitude and stiffness. Exact global feasibility, an explicit bound sharp even for finite multiplicative errors, and failure of each three-channel selection are useful identifiability and measurement-design properties of this normalized center. The value lies in that data-to-model result, not in a new integration or matrix method.
